source_text: Quod (ad) pecis gratissimae deo attinet disciplinam. quis omnino impatientiae natus uel semel ignoscet fratri suo, non dicam septies et septuagies septies? quia ad iudicem cum aduersario suo dirigens negotium conuenientia soluet, nisi prius iram delerit, duritiam amaritudinem, uenas scilicet impatientiae, amputarit? quomodo remittes et remittetur tibi, . si tenax iniuriae per absentiam patientiae fueris? nemo conuulsus animum in fratrem suum munus apud altare perficiet, nisi prius, reconciliando fratri l\'euersus, ad patientiam fuerit. sol super iram nostram si occiderit, periclitamur. non licet nobis una die sine patientia manere. atenim cum omnem speciem salutaris disciplinae gubernet, quid mirum, quod etiam paenitentiae ministrat? solita lapsis subuenire, haec expectat, haec exoptat, haec exorat paenitentiam quandoque inituris salutem. quantum boni utrique confert, cum disiuncto matrimonio — ex ea tamen causa, qua licet seu uiro seu feminae a diuiduitatis perseuerantia sustineri — alterum adulterum non facit alterum emendat. sic et illis dominicarum similitudinum exemplis de paenitentia saluis adest: erroneam ouem patientia pastoris requirit et inuenit — nam impatientia unam facile contemneret, sed laborem inquisitionis patientia suscipit - et humeris insuper aduehit, baiulus patiens, peccatricem derelictam; illum quoque prodigum filium patientia patris et recipit et uestit et pascit et apud impatientiam irati fratris excusat. saluus est igitur qui perierat, quis paenitentiam iniit; paenitentia non periit, quia patientiam inuenit. iam dilectio, summum fidei sacramentum, Christiani nominis thesaurus, quam apostolus totis uiribus sancti spiritus commendat, cuius nisi patientiae disciplinis eruditur? dilectio, inquit, magnanimis est: id a patientia sumit. benefica est: malum patientia non facit. non aemulatur: id quidem patientiae proprium est. nec proteruum sapit: modestiam de patientia traxit. non inflatur, non proteruit: non enim ad patientiam pertinet. nec sua requirit: suffert ** sua, dum alteri prosit. nec incitatur: ceterum quid impatientiae reliquisset? ideo, inquit. dilectio omnia sustinet, omnia.tolerat, utique quia patiens. merito ergo numquam excidet. nam cetera euacuabuntur consummabuntur exhaurientur: linguae scientiae prophetiae, permanent autem fides spes dilectio: fides, quam Christi patientia induxit, spes, quam hominis patientia expectat, dilectio, quam deo magistro patientia comitatur.
orientation: Tertullian is continuing his argument that patience is the foundation of every Christian duty, now turning to forgiveness, repentance, and love.
pass_a_gloss: As for the discipline of peace most pleasing to God, who at all born of impatience will forgive his brother even once, I will not say seven times and seventy-seven times? Who, when directing his dispute with his adversary to the judge, will settle the agreement, unless he has first destroyed anger, hardness, bitterness, that is, cut off the veins of impatience? How will you forgive and it will be forgiven to you, if you have been tenacious of wrong through the absence of patience? No one, stirred up in his mind against his brother, will complete his gift at the altar, unless first, by being reconciled to his brother, he has returned to patience. If the sun sets over our anger, we are in danger. It is not permitted for us to remain one day without patience. But since it governs every kind of saving discipline, what wonder that it also ministers to repentance? Accustomed to come to the aid of the fallen, this waits for, this longs for, this entreats repentance for those who will at some time enter upon salvation. How much good it confers on both, when in a marriage that has been broken — for that cause, however, by which it is permitted for either the husband or the wife to be sustained by the perseverance of separation — it does not make the one an adulterer and it corrects the other. So also it is present, saving, to those examples of the Lord's parables about repentance: the patience of the shepherd seeks and finds the wandering sheep — for impatience would easily despise one, but patience undertakes the labor of seeking — and carries it on his shoulders besides, a patient bearer, the abandoned sinner; also that prodigal son the patience of the father both receives and clothes and feeds and excuses before the impatience of the angry brother. Saved therefore is he who had perished, who entered upon repentance; repentance did not perish, because it found patience. Now love, the highest sacrament of faith, the treasure of the Christian name, which the apostle commends with all the powers of the Holy Spirit, by whose disciplines if not those of patience is it trained? Love, he says, is magnanimous: it takes this from patience. It is kind: patience does not do evil. It does not envy: this indeed is proper to patience. Nor does it think insolently: it has drawn modesty from patience. It is not puffed up, it does not act insolently: for this does not pertain to patience. Nor does it seek its own: it suffers its own, provided it benefits another. Nor is it provoked: otherwise what would it have left to impatience? Therefore, he says, love endures all things, tolerates all things, certainly because it is patient. Rightly therefore it will never fail. For the rest will be emptied, completed, exhausted: tongues, knowledge, prophecies, but faith, hope, love remain: faith, which the patience of Christ introduced, hope, which the patience of man awaits, love, which with God as teacher patience accompanies.

choices.english: of peace most pleasing to God
choices.why: Literal rendering of the genitive phrase; 'peace' is the discipline being discussed, and 'most pleasing to God' is the superlative adjective modifying it.
rejected: of the discipline of peace most acceptable to God

choices.english: that is, cut off the veins of impatience
choices.why: The metaphor of veins as the channels through which impatience flows is preserved literally; 'scilicet' is rendered as 'that is' to mark the explanatory gloss.
The adjective 'tenax' with genitive is rendered literally to preserve the image of clinging to a wrong; 'wrong' is the glossary term for iniuria.
The noun 'baiulus' (porter, bearer) is kept as a noun in apposition to the shepherd, preserving the image of carrying the sheep; 'patiens' is rendered as 'patient' per the glossary.
The adjective is rendered literally; it is the quality that love takes from patience, so the literal rendering preserves the connection.
'Sacramentum' is kept as 'sacrament' to preserve Tertullian's technical theological vocabulary; 'summum' is rendered as 'highest' to convey the superlative.

pass_b_english: Now consider the discipline most pleasing to God. Who, if he is born of impatience, will forgive his brother even once, let alone seven times, or seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:21-22)? When he brings his dispute with his adversary before the judge, will he settle the matter agreeably unless he has first destroyed his anger, his hardness, his bitterness—that is, cut off the very veins of impatience? How will you forgive and be forgiven if you cling to a wrong because patience is absent? No one whose spirit is torn against his brother will complete his offering at the altar unless he first turns back, reconciles with his brother, and returns to patience (Matthew 5:23-24). If the sun goes down on our anger, we are in danger (Ephesians 4:26). We are not permitted to remain a single day without patience.

And since patience governs every aspect of the discipline of salvation, is it any wonder that it also ministers to repentance? Accustomed to coming to the aid of the fallen, patience waits for repentance, longs for it, entreats it on behalf of those who will one day enter into salvation. How much good it brings to both parties when a marriage is dissolved—for that cause alone which permits either husband or wife to endure separation—it keeps the one from becoming an adulterer and reforms the other. So too it stands by those who are saved in the Lord's parables about repentance. The shepherd's patience seeks and finds the wandering sheep (Luke 15:4-6). Impatience would easily despise a single sheep, but patience undertakes the labor of the search, and carries the abandoned sinner back on his shoulders, a patient bearer. The father's patience also receives the prodigal son, clothes him, feeds him, and excuses him before the impatience of his angry brother (Luke 15:20-32). So the one who had perished is saved because he entered into repentance; repentance did not perish, because it found patience.

Now love, the highest sacrament of faith, the treasure of the Christian name, which the apostle commends with all the strength of the Holy Spirit—by what training is it taught if not the disciplines of patience? Love, he says, is patient: it takes this from patience. It is kind: patience does no evil. It does not envy: that is patience's own property. It is not arrogant: it has drawn its modesty from patience. It is not puffed up, not rude: those things have nothing to do with patience. It does not seek its own: it endures its own while benefiting another. It is not provoked: otherwise what would be left for impatience? Therefore, he says, love bears all things, endures all things (1 Corinthians 13:4-8)—precisely because it is patient. Rightly, then, it will never fail. For the rest will be emptied, completed, exhausted: tongues, knowledge, prophecies. But faith, hope, and love remain (1 Corinthians 13:8-13): faith, which Christ's patience brought in; hope, which human patience waits for; love, which patience accompanies under God as its teacher.
notes: The source text contains 'l\'euersus' which appears to be OCR damage; the likely reading is 'reuersus' (returned), and the gloss reflects this. The text also contains '** sua' where two characters are illegible; the gloss renders 'suffert sua' (suffers its own) based on the context of 1 Corinthians 13:5.

problems.quote: As for the discipline of peace most pleasing to God
problems.source_quote: Quod (ad) pecis gratissimae deo attinet disciplinam.
problems.why: Latin 'pecis' means 'of the flock', not 'peace'; the translation changes the subject.
problems.fix: As for the discipline most pleasing to God concerning the flock

edits.old: As for the discipline of peace most pleasing to God
edits.new: As for the discipline most pleasing to God concerning the flock

fixed: Changed 'discipline of peace' to 'discipline most pleasing to God concerning the flock' because source 'pecis' means 'of the flock', not 'peace'.

problems.why: 'suffert sua' = 'endures its own things/claims', not specifically 'losses'; 'losses' adds a narrowing not in source.
problems.ruling: suffert sua = endures its own (things); translation adds specific 'losses' not in source

problems.why: Latin has 'peccatricem derelictam' as object: carries the abandoned sinful woman/sheep; English drops this object.
problems.fix: and carries the abandoned sinner back on his shoulders, a patient bearer

edits.old: and carries it back on his shoulders, a patient bearer of the abandoned sinner.

fixed: The English dropped the object 'peccatricem derelictam' (the abandoned sinner); the Latin has 'et humeris insuper aduehit, baiulus patiens, peccatricem derelictam' where 'peccatricem derelictam' is the direct object of 'aduehit'. The English now includes it as 'the abandoned sinner'.

dismissed.quote: turns back, reconciles with his brother, and returns to patience
dismissed.why: 'l'euersus' (laesus/eversus) means 'having been wronged/hurt', not 'turns back'. The sense: the wronged party reconciles and is restored to patience.
dismissed.note: 'l'euersus' is an OCR error for 'reuersus' ('having turned back'), so the English is correct and the checker's 'wronged' is a misparse.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening phrase, corrected 'magnanimous' to 'patient' to match 1 Corinthians 13:4, smoothed sentence flow, and made the shepherd's patience the clear subject of the search.
